title: DHCP Options and BOOTP Vendor Extensions
subtitle: The catalogue of tagged settings that DHCP and BOOTP carry to a client.
summary: RFC 2132 lists the options that ride in the last field of a DHCP message and in the vendor field of a BOOTP packet. Each option is a numbered tag, a length and some data, covering the subnet mask, routers, DNS servers, lease times, message types and many more. It collects the older BOOTP vendor extensions and adds new ones, so one list serves both protocols.

eli5.summary: When a computer joins a network, a helper hands it a sheet of numbered answers: where the exit is, who to ask for directions, how long it can stay. This RFC is the official list of every line that may be on that sheet.

questions: what is the dhcp magic cookie
what is the dhcp message type option
what is the difference between dhcp options and bootp vendor extensions

tldr.problem: DHCP and BOOTP need to pass many kinds of settings to a client, and clients and servers need a format they can all read.
tldr.mechanism: Each setting is an option made of a one-byte code, a one-byte length and data, with codes assigned from one shared list.
tldr.outcome: Every DHCP client and server can read the same option numbers, and new options are added by registering them rather than changing the protocol.

today: Every DHCP client and server in use still reads and writes these options, and the numbers in this RFC, such as 1 for subnet mask, 3 for router, 6 for DNS servers, 51 for lease time and 53 for message type, are the ones you see in packet captures. The option list is now kept in an IANA registry and has been extended by later RFCs, including RFC 3442 and RFC 4361. Option 43 and option 60 are still used by vendors to configure devices at boot.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
DHCP, defined in RFC 2131, is the way a host on a TCP/IP network is handed an address and other settings. RFC 2131 describes the conversation. RFC 2132 describes the cargo: the list of options, the tagged items that sit in the last field of every DHCP message and say things like "your subnet mask is this" or "your DNS servers are these".

The same list is also the format of the "vendor information" field of a BOOTP packet (RFC 951), so one document serves both protocols. It collects the vendor extensions that RFC 1497 had defined for BOOTP, adds new ones, and supersedes RFC 1497 as the home of the definitions. It obsoletes RFC 1533, the earlier version of this list.

The RFC says that every option except those in its section 9 may be used with either DHCP or BOOTP. The section 9 options are specific to DHCP.
sections.eli5: When you move into a new house the owner hands you a sheet: the door code, where the bins go, the Wi-Fi name. DHCP is the owner handing over the sheet. This RFC is the list of every line that can appear on the sheet.

sections.title: Motivation
sections.content:
BOOTP's vendor field was open-ended. RFC 1497 had defined a common set of items, but DHCP needed far more of them: not just an address, but lease times, message types and ways for a client to say what it wanted. A single, well-known registry of option numbers let any client talk to any server.

The RFC adds that sites with one server shared among mixed clients may still define their own formats for the field. To make room for that, option codes 128 to 254 are reserved for site-specific use.

The document groups the options by what they configure, so a reader can find them by topic. The table shows the groups and some example codes from each section.
sections.eli5: Without a shared list, every site could write its own kind of note and nobody could read each other's. This RFC says: here is the one official list of what a note may say, and what number each line gets.

sections.title: Option Format
sections.content:
Every option begins with a one-byte tag that says which option it is. Only two options are fixed-length with no data: 0 (pad) and 255 (end), which are a lone tag byte. Every other option follows its tag with a one-byte length, then that many bytes of data. The length does not count the tag and length bytes themselves, so a single option holds at most 255 bytes of data. The RFC also says that any option defined later MUST have a length byte, even if the length is fixed or zero.

All multi-byte numbers are in network byte order. Text is NVT ASCII and SHOULD NOT carry a trailing NULL, although receivers must tolerate one without requiring it.

When the options are carried in BOOTP, the first four bytes of the vendor field are the magic cookie, the value 99.130.83.99 (hex 63.82.53.63), which tells a reader that tagged options follow. The pad option can be used to align later fields on word boundaries, and the end option marks the last valid option, with any remaining bytes filled with pad.
sections.eli5: Each line on the sheet starts with a number saying what kind of line it is, then how long it is, then the answer. Because the length is there, a computer that does not know a line can skip it and read the next.

sections.title: Common Configuration Options
sections.content:
Sections 3 to 8 define the options that describe the network a host has joined. They are the ones nearly every client asks for. The subnet mask (option 1) is a 4-byte value; if both it and the router option appear in a reply, the subnet mask MUST come first. The router option (3) is a list of 4-byte addresses in order of preference, so its length is always a multiple of 4. The domain name server option (6) is a list of DNS servers in the same format, and the domain name option (15) is the suffix the client should use when resolving hostnames.

The host name (12) names the client, the time offset (2) gives the subnet's offset from UTC in seconds as a two's-complement 32-bit integer, and the boot file size and swap server options serve diskless machines. Further options cover IP layer behavior, such as interface MTU (26) and broadcast address (28), and TCP behavior, such as default TTL (37) and keepalive interval (38).

Many options carry raw 32-bit IP addresses. The RFC warns that this can make renumbering harder and discourages it at sites that may need to renumber.
sections.eli5: These are the everyday lines on the sheet: how big the street is, where the exit is, where to ask for directions, and what the neighbourhood is called.

sections.title: DHCP-Specific Options
sections.content:
Section 9 defines options that exist only for DHCP, and these make the lease machinery work. The requested IP address (50) lets a client ask for a particular address. The IP address lease time (51) is a 32-bit unsigned count of seconds, and the renewal (58) and rebinding (59) options give the T1 and T2 intervals, also in seconds, after which the client moves to the RENEWING and REBINDING states.

The DHCP message type (53) is one byte naming what kind of message this is: 1 DHCPDISCOVER, 2 DHCPOFFER, 3 DHCPREQUEST, 4 DHCPDECLINE, 5 DHCPACK, 6 DHCPNAK, 7 DHCPRELEASE and 8 DHCPINFORM. The server identifier (54) is the IP address of the chosen server, and the client identifier (61) is the unique key the server uses to index its bindings; the RFC says it must be unique among clients on a subnet. The parameter request list (55) lets a client list the option codes it wants, and the message (56) carries a text error from a server in a DHCPNAK.

Option overload (52) lets the options spill into the 'file' field, the 'sname' field, or both (values 1, 2 and 3). The maximum DHCP message size (57) is 2 bytes with a minimum value of 576. Vendor class identifier (60) lets a client announce what kind of device it is.
sections.eli5: These are the lines about borrowing: how long you may keep the address, when to ask to keep it longer, what kind of letter this is, and a list of things you want to be told.

sections.title: Vendor-Specific Information
sections.content:
Option 43 is the escape hatch. It carries an opaque block of bytes that only a particular vendor's clients and servers understand. The vendor is indicated by the vendor class identifier (option 60) that the client sent. A server that does not know how to interpret what a client sent MUST ignore it, and a client that does not get the vendor information it wants SHOULD try to work without it, perhaps in a degraded mode.

If a vendor needs to send several items, it SHOULD use the encapsulated form: the bytes inside option 43 are themselves a series of code, length and value items with the same syntax as the main options, with three exceptions. There should be no magic cookie, codes other than 0 or 255 may be redefined by the vendor, and a 255 end marker ends only the encapsulated block, not the whole field.

This design means new device types can be supported without asking for new top-level option numbers.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a maker of printers or phones wants to leave a private message. Option 43 is a sealed envelope inside the sheet that only that maker's machines know how to open.

sections.title: Defining New Options
sections.content:
Section 10 sets out the process for adding to the list. An author devises an option, asks IANA for a number, writes it up as an Internet Draft, and submits it through the IETF standards process, where it is reviewed by the DHC working group or as an independent submission. If it fails to gain acceptance as an Internet Standard, the number is returned to IANA for reassignment.

The RFC says this process ensures that option numbers are allocated by a single authority, that new options get technical review, and that documentation is complete and published.

The process has since moved on, and the list of options is now kept in an IANA registry. RFC 2132 has also been updated by RFC 3442, RFC 3942, RFC 4361, RFC 4833 and RFC 5494. The RFC Editor's index lists RFC 2132 as a Draft Standard.

The Security Considerations section is a single sentence: "Security issues are not discussed in this memo." The base DHCP protocol has no built-in authentication, so options from an untrusted server on the same network should not be assumed to be honest.
sections.eli5: If you want a new line on the sheet, you ask the person who keeps the master list for a number, then write down what the line means and let others check it.

data.title: General DHCP option (example: router, code 3, two routers)

fields.name: Code
fields.desc: The tag that identifies the option. 0 (pad) and 255 (end) are the only options with no length or data.

fields.name: Len
fields.desc: Number of data bytes that follow, not counting the code and length bytes. Required for every option except 0 and 255.

fields.name: Address 1
fields.desc: First router address, in order of preference (a1 a2 a3 a4).

fields.name: Address 2
fields.desc: Second router address (a1 a2 a3 a4). The router option length is always a multiple of 4.

data.title: Vendor field carrying options (hex)
data.code:
63 82 53 63        magic cookie (99.130.83.99)
01 04 ff ff ff 00  option 1  subnet mask  255.255.255.0
03 04 c0 00 02 01  option 3  router       192.0.2.1
00                 option 0  pad
ff                 option 255 end

items.title: Subnet mask comes first
items.text: If a reply has both a subnet mask and a router option, the subnet mask MUST be first.

items.title: Lists in preference order
items.text: Router, DNS and other server lists are 4-byte addresses, listed in order of preference.

items.title: Length is a multiple of 4
items.text: Address-list options have a length that is always a multiple of 4, with a minimum of 4.

items.title: Network byte order
items.text: All multi-byte values, such as lease times and the time offset, are in network byte order.

messages.label: DHCPDISCOVER: option 53 = 1, option 55 lists wanted options
DHCPOFFER: option 53 = 2, option 54 server ID, option 51 lease time
DHCPREQUEST: option 53 = 3, option 54 picks the server
DHCPACK: option 53 = 5 plus the requested options, such as 1, 3 and 6
messages.note: The RFC defines the options; RFC 2131 defines this exchange.
